In a panel I am usually the one who says the least, and I decide more than people expect. What I write down is not the answer. It is who the candidate is talking to. The ones who do this badly answer only the person who asked, and the rest of us stop listening within a minute. The ones who do it well look at the person who asked, give the first line to them, and then give the rest to the room. The other thing I write down is what happens when two of us ask about the same thing. If the candidate gives a different answer the second time, that is a bigger problem for me than a weak answer given twice. Consistency is the only thing four people can compare afterwards.

Panels overlap, and we know it. Two of us will ask about the same decision from different angles, and a third will ask it again at the end because he was writing when you answered. The candidates who survive that do one small thing: they say out loud that the question has come up before, without any irritation, and they give the same answer in the same words. Something like, that is the same decision we were discussing earlier, and the number is still sixty days. It sounds obvious. Almost nobody does it. What most people do is add something new the second time, to make it more interesting, and that is when four people start comparing notes and finding two versions.
